panels.rationale: Sagittal MRI from a patient with clinically captioned Stage 3 cystocele and severe anterior vaginal wall/bladder prolapse; arrows annotate cervical elongation and the external urethral meatus. The panel is a real patient MRI, not a diagram, and directly supports cystocele.
panels.attribution_text: Yoshida Ueno et al. Close Contact Transillumination Light Guides Surgeon to Vaginal Point Aa: Pharus Method for Robot-Assisted Sacrocolpopexy.. Asian journal of endoscopic surgery 2025. doi:10.1111/ases.13412. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: MRI sagittal view. The red arrows indicate uterine cervix and cervical elongation. The anterior vaginal wall, in conjunction with the bladder filled with urine, had undergone a severe prolapse, resulting in a Stage 3 cystocele. The yellow arrow indicates the external urethral meatus. The vaginal point Aa, indicated by a green symbol, was situated 3 cm proximal to the external urethral meatus.
in_text_mentions: The Pharus or ICG method was observed to have no adverse effects on any of the patients. The clinical characteristics of the patients are presented in Table 1. The thickness of the vaginal wall at the point Aa was estimated to be between 3.3 and 4.6 mm based on the preoperative MRI scans (Table 2). A sagittal MRI of a typical Stage III patient (Case 4) is shown in Figure 2. In the patient who exhibited severe vaginal prolapse and cervical elongation, as illustrated here, dissection of the vesicovaginal space was anticipated to be a challenging procedure.

The proximity to the bladder and tendency for easy bleeding were evident. plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Nullipara with substantial cystocele'; panel A is a translabial ultrasound at rest showing bladder (B) and urethra (U).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient translabial ultrasound from a figure explicitly describing a substantial cystocele; panel A is the rest view with labeled bladder and urethra. B: Valsalva translabial ultrasound panel demonstrating the cystocele in a nullipara. C: Rest translabial ultrasound panel with bladder neck marked, part of the same cystocele case. D: Valsalva translabial ultrasound with annotated descent of bladder and bladder neck, directly supporting cystocele.
panels.attribution_text: Dietz et al. Pelvic organ prolapse in nulliparae.. The Australian & New Zealand journal of obstetrics & gynaecology 2022. doi:10.1111/ajo.13481. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Nullipara with substantial cystocele and intact retrovesical angle. This is a much rarer situation. Panels A and C are at rest, panels B and D on Valsalva manoeuvre. The vertical line in Panel C shows the position of the bladder neck at rest, vertical lines in Panel D demonstrate (from left to right) descent of the bladder, the bladder neck and the rectal ampulla. S, symphysis pubis; U, urethra; B, bladder; R, rectal ampulla; A, anal canal.
in_text_mentions: scent to 10 mm or more below the symphysis pubis (SP), uterine descent to 15 mm or less above the SP, and rectal descent to 15 mm or more below the SP. A true rectocele (ie a defect of the rectovaginal septum) was diagnosed if there was a discontinuity of the anterior rectal muscularis layer with the internal anal sphincter on Valsalva manoeuvre, of at least 10 mm in depth. 24 Figure 1 illustrates the commonest form of prolapse in vaginally nulliparous women, ie a ‘true’ rectocele. Figure 2 shows a much less common situation: a nullipara with a moderate cystocele and intact retrovesical angle.

panels.rationale: Single-panel parasagittal MRI of a real human patient from a case report titled 'Scrotal Cystocele in a Sliding Left Inguinoscrotal Hernia'; the caption and in-text mentions state the MRI confirmed bladder herniation, i.e. a scrotal cystocele, matching the configured disease cystocele. The manifestation (bladder herniated into the inguinoscrotal sac) is directly supported by panel-specific caption evidence. Scrotal cystocele is an uncommon form, hence typicality 'variant'. No skin is visible so skin tone is null; no age or ethnicity is stated in the caption/in-text. [raw subtype: scrotal cystocele (inguinoscrotal bladder herniation)]
panels.attribution_text: Mohan and Srinivasan. Scrotal Cystocele in a Sliding Left Inguinoscrotal Hernia: A Case Report and Review of Literature.. Euroasian journal of hepato-gastroenterology 2017. doi:10.5005/jp-journals-l0018-1220. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3:.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging (parasagittal section) showing left inguinoscrotal bladder herniation
in_text_mentions: Clinical examination showed a huge soft left inguinoscrotal swelling (Fig. 1). On per rectal examination, he had mild prostatomegaly. A diagnosis of bladder hernia was made on the basis of symptoms. Ultrasound of the left groin reported indirect inguinal hernia with bladder as content, voiding cystourethrogram, and MRI confirmed bladder herniation (Figs 2 and 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal CT of a real patient showing a massive right-sided scrotal cystocele, matching the caption 'CT images of the abdomen and pelvis, in a coronal view (A) ... showing a massive right-sided scrotal cystocele' and the article title 'Incidentally detected massive scrotal cystocele.' The CT finding of bladder descent into the scrotum is not covered by the provided vocabulary (which lists MRI, ultrasound and cystography cystocele signs), so it is given as a proposed finding. [raw subtype: scrotal cystocele (inguinoscrotal bladder herniation)] B: Sagittal CT panel of the same real patient showing the massively herniated contrast-filled bladder extending into the scrotum, per caption '...in sagittal views (B,C), showing a massive right-sided scrotal cystocele.' [raw subtype: scrotal cystocele (inguinoscrotal bladder herniation)] C: Second sagittal CT panel of the same real patient demonstrating the massive right-sided scrotal cystocele...

in_text_mentions: sified as non-Hodgkin lymphoma. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis, performed for staging, revealed an unsuspected massive inguinoscrotal hernia of the urinary bladder, a condition known as scrotal cystocele (Figures 1 and 2). The CT scan also showed moderate right-sided uronephrosis, which was attributed to extrinsic compression of the right ureter. The results of the urinalysis were unremarkable. After work-up of the non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a hernia reduction followed by inguinal herniorrhaphy was planned in order to prevent long-term complications of bladder herniation.
